\chapter{Weather}
\label{ch:hi-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what the weather is doing in Hindi and stay out of the \hi{बारिश} / \hi{वर्षा} false-friend trap.}

Say \hi{मौसम}, then \hi{गर्मी} \hi{है} and \hi{ठंड} \hi{है}, and keep everyday \hi{बारिश} apart from formal \hi{वर्षा} despite the resemblance.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mausam / garmī hai / ṭhanḍ hai …]{\hi{मौसम} — another Perso-Arabic loan, and a false-friend trap}

\label{lesson:HI-C20-mausam}



\begin{quote}
You've already seen Hindi borrow \emph{umr} from Arabic. Here's another one — and this time, English borrowed the SAME root too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{मौसम} — the same root as \textquotedblleft{}monsoon\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{मौसम}} (\emph{mausam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — borrowed from Classical \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{موسم}} (\emph{mawsim}), itself from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{مَوْسِم}} (\emph{mawsim}, \textquotedblleft{}season, time of year, occasion\textquotedblright{}; likely originally used by Arab sailors for seasonal winds). This is the \textbf{exact same root} that gave English \textbf{monsoon} — carried into English in the \textbf{1580s}, well before the British Raj, via \textbf{Portuguese and Dutch} traders in the Indian Ocean spice trade (Portuguese \emph{monção}, Dutch \emph{monssoen}, both from this same Arabic \emph{mawsim}). So \textquotedblleft{}monsoon\textquotedblright{} and Hindi's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} are, quite directly, the same word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{गर्मी} \hi{है}, \hi{ठंड} \hi{है} — heat and cold, native words}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{गर्मी} \hi{है।}} — \textquotedblleft{}It's hot.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there is heat}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{garmī hai.}) \textbf{\hi{ठंड} \hi{है।}} — \textquotedblleft{}It's cold.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there is cold}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ṭhanḍ hai.})
\end{quote}

Both use ordinary Hindi nouns (\textbf{\hi{गर्मी}}, \textquotedblleft{}heat\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{\hi{ठंड}}, \textquotedblleft{}cold\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}, \textquotedblleft{}is/there is\textquotedblright{}) — simpler in shape than Arabic's fully verbless pattern, since Hindi still needs \emph{hai} here.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{बारिश} vs. \hi{वर्षा} — a genuine false-friend trap}
Hindi has \textbf{two} words for \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{} that sound similar enough to assume they're related — \textbf{don't} make that assumption:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{बारिश}} (\emph{baarish}) — from \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{بارش}} (\emph{bāriš}) — the everyday, colloquial word: \textbf{\hi{बारिश} \hi{हो} \hi{रही} \hi{है}} (\textquotedblleft{}it's raining,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}rain is happening\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} (\emph{varṣā}) — fully \textbf{native Sanskrit}, from \textbf{\hi{वर्ष}} (\emph{varṣá}, \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}), tracing to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}wers-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{}) — cousin of Greek \textbf{hérsē} (\textquotedblleft{}dew\textquotedblright{}) and Old Irish \textbf{frass} (\textquotedblleft{}rain-shower\textquotedblright{}). This is the more formal/literary word.
\end{itemize}

Despite the similar sound, dictionaries flag \emph{baarish} and \emph{varṣā} as \textbf{probably not related} — one's a Persian loan, the other a native Sanskrit inheritance from deep in the Indo-European family. A likely false-friend trap, not a confirmed doublet.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mausam\textquotedblright{} — weather, same root as English \textquotedblleft{}monsoon\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}garmī hai. ṭhanḍ hai.\textquotedblright{} — it's hot / it's cold
  \item \textquotedblleft{}baarish hai\textquotedblright{} (everyday) vs. \textquotedblleft{}varṣā\textquotedblright{} (formal) — probably NOT related despite sounding alike
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word shares \hi{मौसम}'s exact root, and how did it reach English? (\textbf{Monsoon} — from Arabic \emph{mawsim} via Persian, carried into English in the 1580s by Portuguese/Dutch traders, well before the British Raj.) Are \textbf{\hi{बारिश}} and \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} related words? (\textbf{Probably not} — despite sounding similar, \emph{baarish} is a Persian loan and \emph{varṣā} is native Sanskrit; dictionaries flag them as likely unrelated.) What PIE root does \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} trace to, and what's its Greek cousin? (\emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}wers-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{} — cousin of Greek \emph{hérsē}, \textquotedblleft{}dew.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dha]{\hi{ध} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S124-letter-dha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{द} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ध}}
\textbf{\hi{ध}} — \emph{dha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{dh}, it is \textbf{dha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an upper spiral ending in a rightward shoulder
  \item a separate lower bowl
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{ध} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{धन्यवाद}} — thank you (dhanyavād — formal, Sanskritic)
  \item \textbf{\hi{सोमवार} \hi{मंगलवार} \hi{बुधवार} \hi{गुरुवार} \hi{शुक्रवार}} — Monday–Friday
  \item \textbf{\hi{दोपहर} \hi{आधी} \hi{रात}} — noon (literally \textquotedblleft{}two pahars,\textquotedblright{} a traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour time unit) and midnight (\textquotedblleft{}half night,\textquotedblright{} fully transparent)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ध}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the upper spiral's inner crossing, curl around the small opening, widen left and down around the outer loop, then sweep right through the shoulder without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at the left waist and sweep down and around the lower bowl to its right junction
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified four-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the loops differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ध}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{ध} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{धन्यवाद}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ध} three times, saying \emph{dha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page and find \hi{ध} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{ध}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{dha}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tha]{\hi{थ} — the last empty seat in a row you have nearly filled}

\label{lesson:HI-S126-letter-tha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{ध} — what does it do?

One character this time. It is the fourth of four, and the other three are already yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{थ}}
\textbf{\hi{थ}} — \emph{tha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{th}, it is \textbf{tha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an upper spiral joined continuously to a broad lower bowl
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

One word you already say ends in it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{हाथ}} — hand (hāth)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: the seat \hi{थ} fills}
Your tongue tip touches the back of your top teeth for all four of these. Two things separate them: whether your voice is switched on, and whether a puff of breath escapes after the release.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{character} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{puff of breath} \\
\midrule
\hi{त} & ta & no \\
\hi{थ} & tha & yes \\
\hi{द} & da & no \\
\hi{ध} & dha & yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You had three of the four seats and one gap. \textbf{\hi{थ}} is the gap, and the shape tells you so: like \hi{ध}, it carries a bowl and a right stem, so the eye that already finds \hi{ध} will find this one.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{थ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the upper spiral's inner-right tip, curl clockwise around the small opening and outward to the left waist, then continue down and clockwise around the broad lower bowl to the right-stem junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may narrow, divide, or simplify the loops differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{थ}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{थ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{हाथ}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}  ·  \hi{धन्यवाद}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{थ} three times, saying \emph{tha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} \hi{त} and then \hi{थ} one after the other, with a hand in front of your mouth, until you feel the puff on the second and not the first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{थ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{tha}}.) Which of the four dental characters puff, and which do not? (\hi{थ} and \hi{ध} puff; \hi{त} and \hi{द} do not.)
\end{tcolorbox}
